name: SAT English Vocab
blurb: Prefixes, suffixes and roots for Reading and Writing

cards.q: What does the prefix "a-, an-" mean?
cards.a: Without, not — negative. Apolitical, amorphous (shapeless), anomalous (not regular), apathy, atypical, anonymous, agnostic, asymmetrical. Before a vowel the Greek form takes the n: anarchy, anesthetic, anomaly.
cards.n: The commonest way a word denies its own root. If you can see the root under it, you can read the word: a- plus morph (shape) is shapeless.

cards.q: What does the prefix "un-" mean?
cards.a: Not, or reverse the action — negative. Unprecedented, unwarranted, untenable, unequivocal, unassailable, unscrupulous, unsubstantiated.
cards.n: Two of these are negative prefixes on already-negative roots and come out positive: unequivocal (leaving no doubt) and unassailable (cannot be attacked) are both praise.

cards.q: What does the prefix "in-, im-, il-, ir-" mean?
cards.a: Not — negative. Incongruous, ineffable, impartial, implacable, illicit, irrevocable, inadvertent, impervious. The spelling assimilates to the letter after it: im- before b, m, p; il- before l; ir- before r.
cards.n: The single most dangerous prefix on the test, because the same letters also mean "into" (see imbue, incipient). Inflammable does not mean fireproof.

cards.q: What does the prefix "non-" mean?
cards.a: Not — negative, and usually flatter and more neutral than un- or in-. Nonpartisan, nonchalant, nondescript, noncommittal.
cards.n: Non- tends to withhold rather than attack: nonpartisan is not an insult, whereas unscrupulous is.

cards.q: What does the prefix "dis-" mean?
cards.a: Not, apart, or away — negative. Disparate (unequal), discrepancy, disillusioned, dissuade, disparage, disseminate, disinterested.
cards.n: Watch the two senses. In disparage it negates; in disseminate it only scatters. And disinterested means impartial, not bored.

cards.q: What does the prefix "mis-" mean?
cards.a: Wrongly or badly — negative. Misconstrue (interpret wrongly), misanthrope (hater of people), misnomer (a wrong name), misappropriate.
cards.n: Mis- says the action happened but went wrong, which is different from un-, where it did not happen at all.

cards.q: What does the prefix "mal-" mean?
cards.a: Bad or evil — strongly negative. Malicious, maladroit (clumsy), malfeasance (wrongdoing in office), malady, malevolent, malign.
cards.n: Mal- is the harshest of the negative prefixes. If a choice carries it and the sentence is only mildly critical, it is probably too strong.

cards.q: What does the prefix "anti-" mean?
cards.a: Against or opposite — negative. Antithetical (directly opposed), antipathy (strong dislike), antidote, antiquated.
cards.n: Antiquated is the odd one: there anti- is really ante-, before, worn down by spelling.

cards.q: What does the prefix "contra-, contro-, counter-" mean?
cards.a: Against — negative or opposing. Contradict, contravene (act against a rule), controversial, counterintuitive, counterproductive.
cards.n: These mark opposition to something already stated, so they signal a pivot: the sentence has just turned.

cards.q: What does the prefix "ob-, op-, oc-, of-" mean?
cards.a: Against, or in the way of — negative. Obstruct, obstinate, obsolete, oppose, obstreperous (noisily defiant), obfuscate (make unclear).
cards.n: Ob- is obstruction rather than hatred: it blocks. Obfuscate blocks understanding, obstinate blocks persuasion.

cards.q: What does the prefix "de-" mean?
cards.a: Down, away, or remove — usually negative. Debunk, detract, depreciate, denounce, detrimental, demote, decline, descend.
cards.n: De- takes something away. Detract removes credit, depreciate removes value, debunk removes a claim.

cards.q: What does the prefix "se-" mean?
cards.a: Apart or aside — usually negative. Segregate, secede, seclude, sedition.
cards.n: Se- separates one thing from a group, which is why it shows up in politics: secede, sedition.

cards.q: What does the prefix "bene-, bon-" mean?
cards.a: Good or well — positive. Beneficial, benevolent, benefactor, bona fide (in good faith).
cards.n: The clearest positive prefix on the test. If the sentence is praising something, bene- survives.

cards.q: What does the prefix "eu-" mean?
cards.a: Good or pleasant — positive. Euphemism (a pleasant substitute word), eulogy (speech in praise), euphoria, euphonious (pleasant-sounding).
cards.n: Eu- is Greek for well, and it almost always attaches to speech or feeling.

cards.q: What does the prefix "pro-" mean?
cards.a: Forward, or in favour of — usually positive. Proponent, prolific, promote, progressive.
cards.n: Pro- is direction as often as approval: prolific is forth-making, not pro-anything. Read the root before you trust the charge.

cards.q: What does the prefix "super-, sur-, supra-" mean?
cards.a: Above, over, or beyond. Superfluous, supersede, surpass, surfeit, supranational, superficial, surmount.
cards.n: Beyond is not the same as good: superfluous (more than needed) and surfeit (too much) are both mildly negative, and superficial is a criticism.

cards.q: What does the prefix "ultra-, extra-" mean?
cards.a: Beyond. Ultraconservative, extraordinary, extraneous (beside the point), extrapolate.
cards.n: Extraneous shows the trap plainly: beyond the matter at hand means irrelevant, which is negative.

cards.q: What does the prefix "hyper-" mean?
cards.a: Over or excessive — an intensifier, often mildly negative. Hyperbole (overstatement), hypercritical, hyperactive.
cards.n: Its opposite is hypo- (under, too little): hyperthermia and hypothermia are opposite emergencies.

cards.q: What does the prefix "omni-, pan-" mean?
cards.a: All — usually positive or neutral. Omnipresent, omniscient, omnivorous, pandemic, panacea (a cure-all), panoramic.
cards.n: Pan- is the Greek half of the pair and omni- the Latin. A panacea is a cure for everything, which in argument usually means nothing.

cards.q: What can word parts reliably tell you on the SAT, and what can they not?
cards.a: They reliably give three things: whether a word is positive or negative, what part of speech it is, and roughly which direction it points. They will not separate two words that point the same way — nominal and negligible both mean small, and only meaning decides between them.
cards.h: → three things it gives, one it does not
cards.n: Morphology is an elimination tool, not a definition machine. Getting from four choices to two in five seconds is the whole point; do not wait for it to hand you the answer.
x: positive or negative, part of speech, direction

cards.q: Why is "direction" not the same as "charge"?
cards.a: A prefix can point strongly in a direction and still be a criticism. Super-, ultra- and hyper- all mean beyond, and superfluous (more than needed), surfeit (too much) and hyperbole (overstatement) are all negative.
cards.n: This is where students lose the points morphology just won them: they read an intensifier as praise. Beyond enough is a fault.

cards.q: The committee found the argument ______, dismissing it in a single sentence. Which of cogent, specious, untenable, meticulous survive on charge alone?
cards.a: Specious and untenable. The sentence is negative (dismissed in a single sentence), so cogent and meticulous are gone before meaning is considered — two of four eliminated in about a second.
cards.n: Then meaning decides: untenable (cannot be held) fits a claim that collapses; specious means plausible but false, which the sentence does not say.

cards.q: Roughly what is a vocabulary question worth if word parts only get you to a coin flip?
cards.a: About 20 points. Two-choice guessing across the six or so Words in Context questions is worth roughly that much, which is why charge alone is worth learning even when it never names the answer.
cards.n: The argument for prefixes is not elegance, it is arithmetic: half of six questions is three, and three questions is a score band.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-tion, -sion, -ation" do to a word?
cards.a: Makes a noun — the act or the result of it. Admonition, habituation, coalition, provocation, derivation, concession.
cards.n: The commonest noun ending in English. If the blank follows "the" or "a", this is the shape you want.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-ment" do to a word?
cards.a: Makes a noun — the act, or the thing produced. Abatement, discernment, predicament, impediment, embellishment.
cards.n: Often built straight onto a verb you already know: abate becomes abatement, discern becomes discernment.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-ity, -ty" do to a word?
cards.a: Makes a noun — the state or quality of. Vulnerability, austerity, ambiguity, integrity, alacrity, veracity.
cards.n: It usually sits on an adjective: ambiguous becomes ambiguity. If you know the adjective, you know the noun.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-ness" do to a word?
cards.a: Makes a noun — the state or quality of, on a plainer, more Germanic base. Forthrightness, thoroughness, bleakness.
cards.n: Where -ity attaches to Latin adjectives, -ness attaches to plain English ones. Same job, different register.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-ance, -ence, -ancy, -ency" do to a word?
cards.a: Makes a noun — the state or quality of. Insolvency, reluctance, benevolence, discrepancy, prudence, deference.
cards.n: The a and e spellings are not a meaning difference, only a difference in which Latin verb the word came from.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-ism" do to a word?
cards.a: Makes a noun — a doctrine, a practice, or a habit of mind. Skepticism, altruism, empiricism, dogmatism.
cards.n: On the SAT it usually names a stance in an argument, which is why it shows up in the humanities passages.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-ure" do to a word?
cards.a: Makes a noun — the act or its result. Conjecture, exposure, composure, overture.
cards.n: Conjecture is the useful one: con- (together) plus ject (throw), a guess thrown together.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-age" do to a word?
cards.a: Makes a noun — a collective thing, or the result of an action. Patronage, verbiage, salvage.
cards.n: Verbiage is a quiet insult: an -age heap of words.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-cy" do to a word?
cards.a: Makes a noun — the state, quality, or office of. Efficacy, complacency, advocacy, intricacy.
cards.n: Efficacy (whether a thing works) is not efficiency (whether it wastes anything). Science passages use both.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-itude" do to a word?
cards.a: Makes a noun — the state or quality of. Fortitude, aptitude, magnitude, platitude.
cards.n: A platitude is flatness made into a noun: a remark so level it carries nothing.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-er, -or, -ist, -ian, -ee, -ant, -ent" do to a word?
cards.a: Makes a noun naming a person or agent. Benefactor, empiricist, historian, nominee, proponent, informant.
cards.n: The -ee form is the one it is done to (nominee), the rest are the one who does it. That asymmetry is occasionally the whole question.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-y, -ry" do to a word?
cards.a: Makes a noun — a practice, a condition, or a body of something. Rivalry, mimicry, scrutiny, tyranny, bravery.
cards.n: Do not confuse it with the adjective -y (bumpy). The base tells you which: mimic is a verb, so mimicry is a noun.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-ous, -ious, -eous" do to a word?
cards.a: Makes an adjective — having the quality of, or full of. Malicious, innocuous, amorphous, ubiquitous, superfluous, tenuous, incongruous.
cards.n: The workhorse adjective ending on this test. Four of the six most-repeated hard words end in it.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-ive" do to a word?
cards.a: Makes an adjective — tending to, having the nature of. Speculative, elusive, incisive, pervasive, combative.
cards.n: It describes a tendency rather than a state, which is why it pairs so often with verbs: speculate, elude, pervade.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-al, -ial, -ical" do to a word?
cards.a: Makes an adjective — relating to. Nominal, detrimental, paradoxical, ephemeral, cynical.
cards.n: The most neutral adjective ending: it says the word is about something, and leaves the charge to the root.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-ic" do to a word?
cards.a: Makes an adjective — relating to, or characteristic of. Idiosyncratic, prolific, dynamic, endemic, pragmatic.
cards.n: Compare -ical carefully: economic and economical are not the same word.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-able, -ible" do to a word?
cards.a: Makes an adjective — capable of being, or fit to be. Amenable, feasible, mutable, plausible, negligible, viable, vulnerable.
cards.n: It turns a verb into a possibility. Negligible is what can be neglected; viable is what can live.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-ful, -less" do to a word?
cards.a: Makes an adjective — full of, or without. Resourceful, remorseless, groundless.
cards.n: Groundless is the useful one in an argument passage: a claim with nothing under it.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-ary" do to a word?
cards.a: Makes an adjective — relating to, or of the nature of. Rudimentary, arbitrary, exemplary, sedentary.
cards.n: Arbitrary is chosen by will alone, not by reason — in a science passage it is always a criticism of a method.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-ory" do to a word?
cards.a: Makes an adjective — having the function or effect of. Cursory, perfunctory, illusory, contradictory.
cards.n: Cursory (running over) and perfunctory (done merely to get through) are both quiet insults about effort.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-ant, -ent" do to a word?
cards.a: Makes an adjective — performing or showing. Prevalent, salient, incipient, prescient, pertinent, defiant.
cards.n: These are also noun endings (an applicant, a proponent). The slot in the sentence decides which you are looking at.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-ish" do to a word?
cards.a: Makes an adjective — somewhat, or in the manner of, often diminishing. Greenish, selfish, bookish, waggish.
cards.n: It hedges. If a sentence wants a firm quality, an -ish word is usually too weak to be the answer.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-esque" do to a word?
cards.a: Makes an adjective — in the style of. Picturesque, Kafkaesque, grotesque.
cards.n: It attaches to names, which is why it is the ending you see in criticism and reviews.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-id" do to a word?
cards.a: Makes an adjective — in a state of. Intrepid, lucid, vapid, morbid, torpid, insipid.
cards.n: A cluster of these are flatness words: vapid, insipid, torpid all mean some version of lifeless.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-ile" do to a word?
cards.a: Makes an adjective — capable of, or inclined to. Fragile, docile, volatile, versatile, puerile.
cards.n: Puerile (boyish, childish) is the one the test likes, and it is always a criticism.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-ize, -ise" do to a word?
cards.a: Makes a verb — to make, or to treat as. Scrutinize, minimize, characterize, temporize, polarize.
cards.n: Temporize is the one worth knowing: to make time, meaning to stall.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-ify, -fy" do to a word?
cards.a: Makes a verb — to make or cause to become. Rectify, exemplify, nullify, mystify, classify.
cards.n: Rectify is rect (straight) plus -ify: to make straight, to set right.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-ate" do to a word?
cards.a: Makes a verb — to cause or to do. Exacerbate, mitigate, substantiate, extricate, perpetuate, replicate.
cards.n: It is also an adjective and a noun ending (a delicate balance, a certificate), so the slot has to decide.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-en" do to a word?
cards.a: Makes a verb — to make or become. Heighten, weaken, harden, lengthen.
cards.n: The plain English counterpart to -ify. Same job on a Germanic base.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-esce, -escent" do to a word?
cards.a: The verb form means to begin or to grow: acquiesce, coalesce, effervesce. The adjective -escent means beginning to be: nascent, obsolescent, convalescent, incandescent.
cards.n: Obsolescent is not obsolete: one is going out of use, the other is already out. Science passages use the difference.

cards.q: Which suffixes make adverbs?
cards.a: -ly is the main one (ostensibly, tacitly, ostentatiously). -wise means in the manner of (likewise, otherwise), and -ward or -wards gives direction (untoward, outward).
cards.n: Untoward is the odd member: it means unfortunate or improper, not a direction at all.

cards.q: Why is "-ate" three different endings?
cards.a: It makes a verb (to advocate), an adjective (a delicate balance) and a noun (a certificate). Only the slot decides: "The committee will ______ for reform" needs the verb advocate, while "a passionate ______ for reform" needs the noun.
cards.h: → three parts of speech, one example each
cards.n: This is the ending most likely to appear four times in one Form, Structure and Sense question.

cards.q: Why can "-ant" and "-ent" not settle a part of speech by themselves?
cards.a: They make both nouns and adjectives. The applicant and the proponent are people; a prevalent view and a salient detail are qualities. Nothing in the ending tells you which — the sentence slot does.
cards.h: → the ambiguity and how to resolve it
cards.n: If two choices share this ending, the suffix has told you nothing and you must go to meaning.

cards.q: When do "-ic" and "-ical" mean different things?
cards.a: Often enough to matter. Economic relates to the economy, economical means thrifty. Historic means important in history, historical means merely of the past. Classic means definitive, classical means of antiquity. Politic means shrewd, political means of politics.
cards.n: A historic decision and a historical decision are not the same claim, and the SAT has used exactly that pair.

cards.q: On a feeling word, what is the difference between "-ed" and "-ing"?
cards.a: -ed describes the one who experiences the feeling; -ing describes the thing that causes it. The audience was bored, because the lecture was boring.
cards.n: Reverse them and you have said the audience causes boredom, which is a different sentence and usually the wrong answer.
x: -ed is the experiencer, -ing is the cause

cards.q: Which pairs differ by one letter and by part of speech?
cards.a: Loath (adjective, reluctant) and loathe (verb, to hate). Prophecy (noun) and prophesy (verb). Advice (noun) and advise (verb). Effect (noun) and affect (verb).
cards.h: → four pairs with parts of speech
cards.n: He was loath to sign, and he loathes paperwork. Both are correct, and swapping them is a grammar error, not a vocabulary one.

cards.q: Why does "-less" not always mean "without value"?
cards.a: Because it can mean beyond, not lacking. Priceless means beyond price and invaluable means beyond value — both mean extremely valuable, the opposite of what the ending suggests.
cards.n: Same trap in both directions: -less can be praise, and in- can be praise.

cards.q: The two accounts ______ in three important respects. Choose between differ, different, difference, differently.
cards.a: Differ. The slot after a subject and before a prepositional phrase needs a verb, and only differ is one — no meaning required.
cards.n: The same four words with a different frame give a different answer: "The ______ between the accounts is minor" takes the noun, difference.

cards.q: The ______ between the accounts is minor. Choose between differ, different, difference, differently.
cards.a: Difference. After "the" and before a prepositional phrase, the slot needs a noun.
cards.n: Form, Structure and Sense questions are grammar questions wearing a vocabulary costume. Read the slot, not the words.

cards.q: What does the prefix "ad-, ac-, af-, ag-, al-, ap-, as-, at-" mean?
cards.a: To, or toward. Adhere, admonish, accede, affable, aggregate, appease, assert. The d assimilates to whatever letter follows.
cards.n: One prefix wearing eight spellings. If a word starts with a doubled consonant, ad- is usually hiding under it: ac-cede, af-fable, ag-gregate.

cards.q: What does the prefix "ab-, abs-" mean?
cards.a: Away from. Abdicate, abstain, abstract, aberrant, absolve.
cards.n: The exact opposite of ad-. Abstain is to hold away from; abdicate is to proclaim oneself away from an office.

cards.q: What does the prefix "ex-, e-, ec-, ef-" mean?
cards.a: Out of. Extricate, evacuate, elicit, expunge, eccentric, effusive, extrapolate.
cards.n: Very common and very readable: elicit draws a response out, extricate gets you out, expunge wipes out.

cards.q: What does the prefix "in-, im-, en-, em- (into)" mean?
cards.a: Into, in, or cause to be. Imbue, incipient, intrinsic, engender, entitle, empower, inundate.
cards.n: These are the same letters as the negative in-, and this is the trap that makes inflammable mean flammable. Check the root before you assume a negation.

cards.q: What does the prefix "inter-" mean?
cards.a: Between or among. Intercede, intervene, intermittent, interdisciplinary.
cards.n: Do not confuse it with intra- (within): an intramural game is inside one school, an intercollegiate one is between schools.

cards.q: What does the prefix "intra-, intro-" mean?
cards.a: Within, or inward. Intramural, introspective, introvert.
cards.n: Intrinsic belongs to this family: a quality within the thing itself.

cards.q: What does the prefix "sub-, sup-, sus-, suc-, suf-" mean?
cards.a: Under, below, or secretly. Substantiate, subtle, supplant, supplement, subversive, sustain, succumb.
cards.n: Substantiate is literally to stand under: to put something underneath a claim so it holds.

cards.q: What does the prefix "trans-" mean?
cards.a: Across, through, or change. Transcend, transient, transmute, transparent.
cards.n: Transient is across time rather than space: passing through, not staying.

cards.q: What does the prefix "circum-, peri-" mean?
cards.a: Around. Circumvent, circumspect, circumscribe, perimeter, peripheral.
cards.n: Circumspect is looking around before acting, which is why it means cautious rather than nosy.

cards.q: What does the prefix "per-" mean?
cards.a: Through, or thoroughly. Pervasive, perpetuate, pertinent, perfunctory, permeate.
cards.n: The thoroughly sense is the useful one: perspicacious is seeing right through something.

cards.q: What does the prefix "dia-" mean?
cards.a: Through or across. Diameter, dialogue, diagnose, diametric.
cards.n: Dialogue is talk going across between people, not two people talking (that would need di-).

cards.q: What does the prefix "epi-" mean?
cards.a: Upon or over. Epidemic, epidermis, epitaph, epilogue.
cards.n: An epilogue is the word set upon the end; an epigraph the writing set upon the front.

cards.q: What does the prefix "hypo-" mean?
cards.a: Under, or too little. Hypothesis, hypothermia, hypocritical.
cards.n: The mirror of hyper-. A hypothesis is what is placed under an argument to hold it up while it is tested.

cards.q: What does the prefix "para-" mean?
cards.a: Beside, beyond, or contrary to. Paradox, parallel, paradigm, paramount.
cards.n: The contrary sense makes paradox: para- (against) plus dox (opinion), a thing against what is believed.

cards.q: What does the prefix "meta-" mean?
cards.a: Change, or beyond. Metamorphosis, metaphor, metaphysical.
cards.n: Metamorphosis is change of shape: meta- plus morph. If you know one, you can read the other.

cards.q: What does the prefix "syn-, sym-, syl-, sys-" mean?
cards.a: Together, or same. Synthesis, symbiotic, synchronize, synopsis, idiosyncratic.
cards.n: Synthesis is putting together, which is exactly what the SAT asks for in a synthesis question.

cards.q: What does the prefix "com-, con-, col-, cor-, co-" mean?
cards.a: With, together, or thoroughly. Consensus, conventional, corroborate, collaborate, compound, concede.
cards.n: The thoroughly sense is easy to miss: corroborate is not co-strengthening, it is thoroughly strengthening.

cards.q: What does the prefix "re-" mean?
cards.a: Back, or again. Rescind, refute, resilient, replicate, reconcile, reiterate.
cards.n: Back is the sense that carries the hard words: rescind cuts back, refute beats back, resilient jumps back.

cards.q: What does the prefix "pre-" mean?
cards.a: Before. Prescient, preclude, precedent, precipitate, preemptive.
cards.n: Preclude is to shut before: to stop something in advance, not merely to prevent it now.

cards.q: What does the prefix "ante-" mean?
cards.a: Before, in time or place. Antecedent, antebellum, antedate.
cards.n: The Latin twin of pre-. Antebellum is before the war; an antecedent goes before.

cards.q: What does the prefix "post-" mean?
cards.a: After. Posthumous, postpone, postscript.
cards.n: Posthumous is after burial, which is why it describes work published after a writer dies.

cards.q: What does the prefix "retro-" mean?
cards.a: Backward. Retrospective, retroactive, retrograde.
cards.n: A retrospective looks back; a retroactive rule reaches back.

cards.q: What does the prefix "proto-" mean?
cards.a: First, or earliest. Prototype, protocol, protozoan.
cards.n: A prototype is the first type, the one everything after is measured against.

cards.q: What does the prefix "neo-" mean?
cards.a: New. Neologism, neolithic, neoclassical.
cards.n: A neologism is a newly coined word — the term itself turns up in language passages.

cards.q: What does the prefix "pale-, paleo-" mean?
cards.a: Ancient. Paleolithic, paleontology, paleogenetics.
cards.n: The opposite of neo-. Paleolithic and neolithic are old stone and new stone.

cards.q: What does the prefix "mono-, uni-" mean?
cards.a: One. Monolithic, monotonous, uniform, unilateral.
cards.n: Monolithic is one stone: a thing with no seams, which in an argument means it admits no variation.

cards.q: What does the prefix "bi-, di-, duo-" mean?
cards.a: Two. Bipartisan, bifurcate, dichotomy, dilemma.
cards.n: A dichotomy is a cut in two, and a dilemma is two premises — both are traps in argument passages when the two are false.

cards.q: What does the prefix "tri-" mean?
cards.a: Three. Trivial, tripartite, triad.
cards.n: Trivial is the one to remember: tri- plus via (road), the three-road crossing where everybody met, so what was said there was commonplace.

cards.q: What does the prefix "quadr-, tetra-, penta-, hex-, oct-, dec-" mean?
cards.a: Four, four, five, six, eight, ten. Quadrant, tetrahedron, pentagon, decade.
cards.n: Latin and Greek run in parallel: quadr- and tetra- both mean four, from the two languages.

cards.q: What does the prefix "cent-, milli-, kilo-" mean?
cards.a: Hundred, thousandth, thousand. Century, millimeter, kilometer.
cards.n: Milli- shrinks and kilo- enlarges, which is the only pair here likely to matter in a science passage.

cards.q: What does the prefix "multi-, poly-" mean?
cards.a: Many. Multifaceted, polyglot, polymath, polymorphic.
cards.n: A polymath knows many things; a polyglot speaks many languages. Both are compliments.

cards.q: What does the prefix "semi-, hemi-, demi-" mean?
cards.a: Half, or partly. Semicircle, semiautonomous, hemisphere, demigod.
cards.n: Semi- is the hedging one: semiautonomous is a careful claim, not a strong one.

cards.q: What does the prefix "micro-, mini-" mean?
cards.a: Small. Microcosm, microscopic, minimize.
cards.n: A microcosm is a small world standing for a large one — a favourite word in literature passages.

cards.q: What does the prefix "macro-, mega-" mean?
cards.a: Large. Macroeconomic, megalith.
cards.n: Macro- and micro- mark the scale of a claim, which is often what a social-science passage is arguing about.

cards.q: What does the prefix "olig-" mean?
cards.a: Few. Oligarchy, oligopoly.
cards.n: Rule by a few, or a market held by a few. Both turn up in history and economics passages.

cards.q: What does the prefix "equi-, iso-, homo-" mean?
cards.a: Equal or same. Equilibrium, equivocal, isolate, homogeneous.
cards.n: Equivocal is equal-voiced: it says two things at once, so it means evasive or ambiguous.

cards.q: What does the prefix "hetero-" mean?
cards.a: Different. Heterogeneous, heterodox.
cards.n: The opposite of homo-. Heterodox is a different opinion from the accepted one; orthodox is the straight one.

cards.q: How do you tell the negative "in-" from the "in-" that means "into"?
cards.a: You cannot from the letters — only from the root and the sentence. Incongruous, ineffable and impartial negate; imbue, incipient, inundate and inflammable mean into. Inflammable therefore means it burns easily, not that it is fireproof.
cards.h: → the ambiguity, examples of each, the famous trap
cards.n: This is the one place where a prefix will confidently hand you the wrong answer. If in- gives you a meaning that seems too neat, check the root.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-logy, -ology" mean?
cards.a: Study of, or discourse about. Geology, etymology (the study of word origins), tautology (saying the same thing twice).
cards.n: Tautology is the one that appears in argument questions: a claim that only restates itself proves nothing.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-graph, -graphy, -gram" mean?
cards.a: Writing or recording. Bibliography, cartography, epigram, seismograph. The same piece works inside a word too: epigraph, monograph.
cards.n: A seismograph writes down shaking; a bibliography writes down books.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-meter, -metry" mean?
cards.a: Measure. Barometer, symmetry, geometry.
cards.n: Symmetry is measuring together: the two halves measure the same.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-scope, -scopy" mean?
cards.a: Look at. Microscope, telescope, endoscopy.
cards.n: Related to the root spec / spic, also meaning look — as in circumspect and perspicacious.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-cracy, -crat" mean?
cards.a: Rule, or a ruler. Democracy, technocrat, autocrat, meritocracy.
cards.n: Whatever comes before it is what does the ruling: demo- the people, techno- the experts, merit- the deserving.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-archy, -arch" mean?
cards.a: Rule, or a chief. Oligarchy, anarchy, matriarch, hierarchy.
cards.n: Anarchy is an- (without) plus -archy: without a ruler, not merely disorder.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-cide" mean?
cards.a: Kill. Homicide, pesticide, genocide.
cards.n: From the same root as incisive and scissors: cutting down.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-vore, -vorous" mean?
cards.a: Eat. Herbivore, omnivorous, voracious.
cards.n: Voracious keeps the root without the suffix: devouring, and used of readers as often as of animals.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-phile, -philia" mean?
cards.a: Love of. Bibliophile, francophile, hydrophilic.
cards.n: The opposite of -phobe. A bibliophile loves books; a hydrophilic molecule is drawn to water.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-phobe, -phobia" mean?
cards.a: Fear of. Xenophobia, agoraphobia.
cards.n: Xeno- is stranger and agora- is the marketplace, so the prefix names what is feared.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-pathy, -path" mean?
cards.a: Feeling, suffering, or disease. Empathy, antipathy, apathy, sociopath.
cards.n: The prefix decides everything: em- (in) is feeling with, anti- is feeling against, a- is no feeling at all.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-osis" mean?
cards.a: A condition or a process. Symbiosis, metamorphosis, osmosis.
cards.n: It names something happening over time, which is why biology passages are full of it.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-oid" mean?
cards.a: Resembling. Humanoid, asteroid, tabloid.
cards.n: It says like, not is — and often carries a faint dismissal.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-escent" mean?
cards.a: Beginning to be. Obsolescent, nascent, incandescent, convalescent.
cards.n: Beginning is the whole meaning: nascent is just being born, obsolescent is only starting to go out of use.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-ling, -let, -ette" mean?
cards.a: Small, and sometimes dismissive. Underling, droplet, statuette.
cards.n: The dismissal is the point in an underling: small in rank, said unkindly.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-monger" mean?
cards.a: A dealer in — almost always negative. Fearmonger, warmonger, rumormonger.
cards.n: One of the few endings that carries a charge on its own. If you see it, the sentence is an accusation.

cards.q: What does the suffix "-most, -ward" mean?
cards.a: Direction or extreme. Foremost, untoward, hitherto.
cards.n: Untoward hides in this group and means unfortunate or improper, which is not a direction at all.

cards.q: What does the root "dict" mean?
cards.a: Say. Contradict, edict, dictum, indict.
cards.n: An edict is spoken out by authority; to contradict is to speak against.

cards.q: What does the root "loqu, locu" mean?
cards.a: Speak. Eloquent, loquacious (talkative), circumlocution (talking around), soliloquy.
cards.n: Circumlocution is the SAT-useful one: circum- (around) plus locu, saying a thing the long way instead of saying it.

cards.q: What does the root "voc, vok" mean?
cards.a: Call, voice. Evoke, equivocal, vociferous, revoke.
cards.n: Equivocal is equal-voiced, so it means ambiguous or evasive — and unequivocal, its opposite, is one of the strongest words of certainty on the test.

cards.q: What does the root "fa, fabl, fess" mean?
cards.a: Speak. Affable, ineffable, profess, fable.
cards.n: Ineffable means it cannot be spoken out — beyond words, not merely hard to say.

cards.q: What does the root "scrib, script" mean?
cards.a: Write. Inscribe, prescriptive, circumscribe, conscript.
cards.n: To circumscribe is to draw a line around, so it means to limit — a common move in argument passages.

cards.q: What does the root "cogn, gnos" mean?
cards.a: Know. Recognize, incognito, agnostic, prognosis.
cards.n: A prognosis is knowing beforehand; an agnostic is one without knowledge.

cards.q: What does the root "sci" mean?
cards.a: Know. Prescient, conscientious, omniscient.
cards.n: Prescient is pre- plus sci: knowing in advance, and always a compliment.

cards.q: What does the root "doc, doct" mean?
cards.a: Teach. Docile, indoctrinate, doctrine.
cards.n: Docile means teachable, which is why it describes something easily led rather than merely quiet.

cards.q: What does the root "cred" mean?
cards.a: Believe. Incredulous, credible, credulous, credence.
cards.n: Credulous means too ready to believe; incredulous means unwilling to. One is a fault, the other a reaction.

cards.q: What does the root "dox, dog" mean?
cards.a: Opinion, belief. Orthodox, paradox, heterodox, dogmatic.
cards.n: The prefix decides: ortho- (straight) is accepted belief, hetero- (different) is not, para- (contrary) is self-contradictory.

cards.q: What does the root "log" mean?
cards.a: Word, reason. Logic, epilogue, neologism, apologist.
cards.n: An apologist is not apologizing: it is one who speaks in defence of something.

cards.q: What does the root "put" mean?
cards.a: Think, reckon. Compute, repute, dispute, impute.
cards.n: To impute is to reckon something onto someone — to attribute it, usually a fault.

cards.q: What does the root "rat" mean?
cards.a: Think, reckon. Rational, ratify, ratiocination.
cards.n: To ratify is to confirm by reckoning: to make a thing official by counting the votes.

cards.q: What does the root "cede, ceed, cess" mean?
cards.a: Go, yield. Concede, precedent, accessible, unprecedented, secede.
cards.n: Unprecedented takes three pieces: un- plus pre- plus ced — nothing has gone before it.

cards.q: What does the root "ven, vent" mean?
cards.a: Come. Intervene, conventional, advent, contravene.
cards.n: To contravene is to come against a rule; to intervene is to come between.

cards.q: What does the root "duc, duct" mean?
cards.a: Lead. Conduct, induce, ductile, conducive.
cards.n: Conducive leads together toward a result, so it means helping to bring about.

cards.q: What does the root "mit, miss" mean?
cards.a: Send. Remit, omission, emit, intermittent.
cards.n: Intermittent sends between: stopping and starting, not merely occasional.

cards.q: What does the root "fer" mean?
cards.a: Carry, bear. Infer, confer, vociferous, defer, proffer.
cards.n: Vociferous carries the voice: voc plus fer, loud in complaint.

cards.q: What does the root "port" mean?
cards.a: Carry. Comportment, deport, importune.
cards.n: Comportment is how you carry yourself — bearing, in the old sense.

cards.q: What does the root "ject" mean?
cards.a: Throw. Abject, conjecture, object, interject.
cards.n: Conjecture throws ideas together: a guess, not a conclusion. Science passages use it precisely.

cards.q: What does the root "tract" mean?
cards.a: Pull, draw. Detract, intractable, protracted, abstract.
cards.n: Intractable is not pullable: a problem that will not be moved, or a person who will not be led.

cards.q: What does the root "pel, puls" mean?
cards.a: Drive, push. Compel, repulse, impulsive, dispel.
cards.n: To dispel is to drive apart — you dispel a myth the way wind drives off cloud.

cards.q: What does the root "grad, gress" mean?
cards.a: Step, go. Transgress, digress, retrograde, progressive.
cards.n: To digress is to step away from the path, which is exactly what the SAT means when it asks about a paragraph that wanders.

cards.q: What does the root "cur, curs (run)" mean?
cards.a: Run. Cursory, concur, recur, precursor.
cards.n: Cursory means run over quickly, so it is a criticism of attention. Note there is a second cur- meaning care (curator, accurate).

cards.q: What does the root "flu, flux" mean?
cards.a: Flow. Superfluous, affluent, influx, fluctuate.
cards.n: Superfluous is over-flowing: more than is needed, and therefore a fault.

cards.q: What does the root "vert, vers" mean?
cards.a: Turn. Averse, subvert, inverse, versatile.
cards.n: Averse is turned away from, which is a dislike. Adverse, turned against, is a circumstance. The test uses both.

cards.q: What does the root "plic, plex, ply" mean?
cards.a: Fold. Replicate, complex, explicit, imply.
cards.n: Explicit is folded out — laid open. Implicit is folded in, left to be inferred.

cards.q: What does the root "cip, cap, cept (take)" mean?
cards.a: Take, seize. Incipient, precipitate, perception, susceptible.
cards.n: Incipient takes hold at the start: just beginning. Precipitate takes headlong: sudden, or triggering.

cards.q: What does the root "sal, sil, sult" mean?
cards.a: Jump. Salient, resilient, insult, desultory.
cards.n: Salient jumps out at you; resilient jumps back; desultory jumps away from the point.

cards.q: What does the root "volv, volut" mean?
cards.a: Roll, turn. Convoluted, evolve, involve.
cards.n: Convoluted is rolled together: twisted, and in a passage question it is always a complaint about the writing.

cards.q: What does the root "fac, fic, fect" mean?
cards.a: Make, do. Facilitate, efficacious, artifice, feasible, prolific.
cards.n: Artifice is made by skill and therefore suspect: a trick rather than a craft.

cards.q: What does the root "stru, struct" mean?
cards.a: Build. Obstruct, infrastructure, construe.
cards.n: To construe is to build a meaning out of words, which is why misconstrue means to build the wrong one.

cards.q: What does the root "ten, tain, tin" mean?
cards.a: Hold. Pertinent, tenacious, abstain, untenable, retain.
cards.n: Untenable cannot be held: a position that collapses under pressure. Pertinent holds through to the matter.

cards.q: What does the root "cap, capt (hold)" mean?
cards.a: Hold, take in. Capacious, captivate, incapacitate.
cards.n: Capacious is roomy — able to hold much. Distinguish it from cip / cept, which is seizing rather than containing.

cards.q: What does the root "frag, fract" mean?
cards.a: Break. Fragile, infraction, refractory, fractious.
cards.n: Fractious and refractory both mean unruly: broken away from control.

cards.q: What does the root "rupt" mean?
cards.a: Break. Disrupt, erupt, corrupt.
cards.n: Corrupt is thoroughly broken — the moral sense came from the physical one.

cards.q: What does the root "scind, scis" mean?
cards.a: Cut. Rescind, incisive, excise.
cards.n: Rescind cuts back a decision; incisive cuts into a problem, which is praise.

cards.q: What does the root "sect" mean?
cards.a: Cut. Dissect, intersect, sectarian.
cards.n: A sect is a group cut off from a larger one, which is what makes sectarian a criticism.

cards.q: What does the root "string, strict" mean?
cards.a: Bind, tighten. Stringent, restrict, constrict.
cards.n: Stringent rules bind tightly. It is not a synonym for strict in tone: stringent is neutral and technical.

cards.q: What does the root "solv, solu" mean?
cards.a: Loosen. Insolvent, dissolute, absolve, resolute.
cards.n: Insolvent cannot loosen its debts. Dissolute has come apart morally. Resolute has been loosened and re-tied: firm.

cards.q: What does the root "lig, leag" mean?
cards.a: Bind. Oblige, allegiance, religious.
cards.n: Oblige binds you toward something — a duty, not a favour, in the original sense.

cards.q: What does the root "vit, viv" mean?
cards.a: Life. Vital, vivacious, viable, revive.
cards.n: Viable is able to live, which on the test usually means a plan that can actually work.

cards.q: What does the root "anim" mean?
cards.a: Mind, soul, life. Unanimous, magnanimous, animosity, equanimity.
cards.n: Magnanimous is great-souled: generous, especially toward someone you have beaten. Equanimity is an even soul: calm.

cards.q: What does the root "sens, sent" mean?
cards.a: Feel. Consensus, dissent, sentiment, insensate.
cards.n: Consensus is feeling together and dissent is feeling apart — the two poles of every argument passage.

cards.q: What does the root "val, vail" mean?
cards.a: Worth, strength. Ambivalent, evaluate, prevalent, convalesce.
cards.n: Ambivalent is both-strengths: pulled two ways, not merely uncertain.

cards.q: What does the root "rob, robor" mean?
cards.a: Strength. Corroborate, robust.
cards.n: To corroborate is to strengthen thoroughly — evidence that props up a claim someone else made.

cards.q: What does the root "fort, forc" mean?
cards.a: Strong. Fortitude, force, reinforce.
cards.n: Fortitude is strength made into a noun: endurance under difficulty.

cards.q: What does the root "grat, grac" mean?
cards.a: Pleasing, thankful. Ingratiate, gracious, gratuitous.
cards.n: Gratuitous means given free, and therefore uncalled for — an insult about excess, not generosity.

cards.q: What does the root "suav, suad" mean?
cards.a: Sweet, urge. Assuage, persuade, dissuade.
cards.n: Assuage sweetens: to soothe or ease, most often grief or hunger.

cards.q: What does the root "fid" mean?
cards.a: Faith, trust. Fidelity, perfidious, confide, bona fide.
cards.n: Perfidious is faith gone through and broken: treacherous.

cards.q: What does the root "am, amic" mean?
cards.a: Love. Amiable, amicable, enamored.
cards.n: Amiable describes a person and amicable a settlement — friendly people, friendly agreements.

cards.q: What does the root "vulner" mean?
cards.a: Wound. Vulnerable, invulnerable.
cards.n: Vulnerable is able to be wounded, which is why it takes an object: vulnerable to something.

cards.q: What does the root "morph" mean?
cards.a: Shape. Amorphous, metamorphosis, polymorphic.
cards.n: Amorphous is without shape, and on the test it describes a vague idea more often than a physical thing.

cards.q: What does the root "form" mean?
cards.a: Shape. Uniform, formulaic, conform.
cards.n: Formulaic is a criticism: shaped to a formula, so nothing in it was decided freshly.

cards.q: What does the root "nom, nym" mean?
cards.a: Name, law. Nominal, misnomer, autonomous, synonym, anonymous.
cards.n: The two senses meet in autonomous: self-lawed, governing itself. And nominal is in name only.

cards.q: What does the root "ortho" mean?
cards.a: Straight, correct. Orthodox, orthography, orthopedic.
cards.n: Orthography is correct writing — spelling. Orthodox is correct opinion.

cards.q: What does the root "rect" mean?
cards.a: Straight, right. Rectify, rectitude, direct.
cards.n: Rectitude is straightness of character; rectify is to make a thing straight again.

cards.q: What does the root "equ, iqu" mean?
cards.a: Equal, fair. Equitable, iniquity, equivocal.
cards.n: Iniquity is un-equal: injustice. The vowel shifts but the root is the same.

cards.q: What does the root "par" mean?
cards.a: Equal. Disparate, parity, comparable.
cards.n: Disparate is not equal — fundamentally different, not merely various.

cards.q: What does the root "prob, prov" mean?
cards.a: Test, prove. Probity, reprove, approbation.
cards.n: Probity is proven honesty. Approbation is approval, and it is one of the strongest positive words the test uses.

cards.q: What does the root "temper, tempor" mean?
cards.a: Moderate, time. Temperate, temporize, contemporary, extemporaneous.
cards.n: The two senses share a root through the idea of due measure. To temporize is to play for time.

cards.q: What does the root "greg" mean?
cards.a: Flock, group. Gregarious, segregate, congregate.
cards.n: Gregarious belongs with the flock: sociable, and always a description of a person.

cards.q: What does the root "cert, cern, cret" mean?
cards.a: Sift, separate, be sure. Discern, discrete, ascertain, secret.
cards.n: Discrete (separate) is not discreet (tactful). The test has used both spellings in one question.

cards.q: What does the root "crep" mean?
cards.a: Creak, rattle. Discrepancy, decrepit.
cards.n: A discrepancy is a rattle between two figures that should have matched.

cards.q: What does the root "mut" mean?
cards.a: Change. Mutable, immutable, permutation, commute.
cards.n: Mutable is subject to change, immutable is not — a pair that shows up whenever a passage argues about what is fixed.

cards.q: What does the root "stat, sist, stan" mean?
cards.a: Stand. Substantiate, static, obstinate, persist.
cards.n: Substantiate stands under a claim; obstinate stands in the way. Same root, opposite manners.

cards.q: What does the root "terr" mean?
cards.a: Earth. Subterranean, terrestrial, terrain.
cards.n: Do not confuse it with the terr- of terror, which gives terrific and terrible from the same fear.

cards.q: What does the root "ter, tri (rub)" mean?
cards.a: Rub, wear. Detrimental, attrition, contrite.
cards.n: Detrimental wears something away — real damage over time, not a single blow.

cards.q: What does the root "jur, jud, jus" mean?
cards.a: Law, judge. Adjudicate, perjury, judicious.
cards.n: Judicious is showing good judgement; judicial is of the courts. One is praise, the other is a category.

cards.q: What does the root "cur, cura (care)" mean?
cards.a: Care. Curator, accurate, sinecure.
cards.n: A sinecure is without care: a post that pays without work. Note the other cur-, meaning run (cursory, precursor).

cards.q: What does the root "spec, spic" mean?
cards.a: Look. Circumspect, perspicacious, conspicuous, specious.
cards.n: Specious looks right and is not — the whole meaning is in the root: it is about appearance.

cards.q: What does the root "vid, vis" mean?
cards.a: See. Evident, visionary, supervise, improvise.
cards.n: To improvise is to do a thing not seen beforehand: im- (not) plus pro- (before) plus vis.

cards.q: What does the root "magn, maj, max" mean?
cards.a: Great. Magnanimous, magnitude, maxim.
cards.n: A maxim is a great saying compressed to a line — the kind of sentence a passage will ask you to evaluate.

cards.q: What does the root "min" mean?
cards.a: Small, less. Minimize, diminish, minutiae.
cards.n: Minutiae are the small things, and the word is almost always a complaint about attention spent on them.

cards.q: What does the root "plen, ple, plet" mean?
cards.a: Full. Replenish, plenitude, supplement, deplete.
cards.n: Supplement fills up from underneath: sub- plus ple, an addition that completes.

cards.q: What does the root "grav, grief" mean?
cards.a: Heavy. Gravitas, aggravate, grievous.
cards.n: Aggravate is to make heavier — to worsen, not merely to annoy.

cards.q: What does the root "lev" mean?
cards.a: Light, raise. Alleviate, levity, elevate.
cards.n: Alleviate lightens a burden; levity is lightness of manner. The opposite of grav-.

cards.q: "Invaluable" looks like it means not valuable. What does it actually mean?
cards.a: Too valuable to be measured — extremely valuable.
cards.n: Here in- is an intensifier reaching past value, not a negation of it. Priceless works the same way.

cards.q: "Priceless" looks like it means worthless. What does it actually mean?
cards.a: Beyond price — extremely valuable.
cards.n: The -less means beyond, not lacking. Pair it with invaluable and learn them together.

cards.q: "Inflammable" looks like it means not flammable. What does it actually mean?
cards.a: Flammable — it burns easily.
cards.n: The in- here means into, as in inflame. This is the reason safety labels now say flammable instead.

cards.q: "Disinterested" looks like it means uninterested. What does it actually mean?
cards.a: Impartial — having no personal stake in the outcome.
cards.n: A disinterested judge is the ideal; an uninterested one is asleep. The test uses the correct sense.

cards.q: "Ingenuous" looks like it means not genuine. What does it actually mean?
cards.a: Naive, frank, artless.
cards.n: Its opposite, disingenuous, does mean insincere — so the pair looks backwards and is not.

cards.q: "Impertinent" looks like it means not pertinent. What does it actually mean?
cards.a: Rude, impudent.
cards.n: The older sense of pertinent (belonging, proper) survives in the negative: not proper, therefore cheeky.

cards.q: "Indifferent" looks like it means not different. What does it actually mean?
cards.a: Apathetic, unconcerned.
cards.n: Nothing to do with difference in the modern sense — it is not making a difference between things, so not caring.

cards.q: "Nonplussed" looks like it means unfazed. What does it actually mean?
cards.a: Bewildered, at a loss.
cards.n: From non plus, no more: the point past which you can say nothing further. The casual misuse is now common, but the test uses the real meaning.

cards.q: "Unassuming" looks like it means not assuming things. What does it actually mean?
cards.a: Modest, unpretentious.
cards.n: It is a compliment. The assuming here is putting on airs, not supposing.

cards.q: "Unwitting" looks like it means not clever. What does it actually mean?
cards.a: Unaware, unintentional.
cards.n: Wit once meant knowledge, so unwitting is without knowing — it describes an act, not a person.

cards.q: "Enervate" looks like it means to energize. What does it actually mean?
cards.a: To drain of energy, to weaken.
cards.n: Almost exactly the opposite of what it sounds like, and the SAT knows it. Nerve here means sinew, and e- takes it out.

cards.q: "Noisome" looks like it means noisy. What does it actually mean?
cards.a: Foul-smelling, offensive.
cards.n: From annoy, not from noise. It is about the nose only by coincidence.

cards.q: "Fulsome" looks like it means abundant in a good way. What does it actually mean?
cards.a: Excessive to the point of insincerity.
cards.n: Fulsome praise is a criticism of the praiser. Do not read the full- as generous.

cards.q: "Restive" looks like it means restful. What does it actually mean?
cards.a: Restless, impatient, hard to control.
cards.n: It came from horses refusing to move, and then turned into its near-opposite: fidgeting to move.

cards.q: "Compendious" looks like it means vast, encyclopedic. What does it actually mean?
cards.a: Concise — briefly comprehensive.
cards.n: A compendium covers everything in little space, so the adjective is about brevity, not bulk.

cards.q: "Peruse" looks like it means to skim. What does it actually mean?
cards.a: To read thoroughly and carefully.
cards.n: The casual sense has drifted to the opposite. On the test, to peruse is to read closely.

cards.q: "Specious" looks like it means special. What does it actually mean?
cards.a: Superficially plausible but actually false.
cards.n: The root spec means look: it looks right. A specious argument is the most dangerous kind, because it survives a glance.

cards.q: "Terrific and terrible" looks like it means unrelated in charge. What does it actually mean?
cards.a: Both come from terror. One drifted to praise and one stayed a criticism.
cards.n: A reminder that a shared root guarantees a shared history, not a shared charge.

cards.q: "Prone" looks like it means reluctant. What does it actually mean?
cards.a: Having a tendency toward — or lying face down.
cards.n: Prone to error means likely to make errors. It never means unwilling.

cards.q: "Loath" looks like it means to hate (the verb loathe). What does it actually mean?
cards.a: Reluctant — and it is an adjective.
cards.n: He was loath to sign, and he loathes paperwork. One letter, two parts of speech.

cards.q: "Sanction" looks like it means one thing. What does it actually mean?
cards.a: Both to approve and to penalize. Only context decides.
cards.n: A contronym: sanctions against a country punish, while sanctioning a plan permits it.

cards.q: "Cleave" looks like it means one thing. What does it actually mean?
cards.a: Both to split apart and to cling to. Only context decides.
cards.n: Two different old verbs collapsed into one spelling. The sentence has to tell you which.

cards.q: "Moot" looks like it means settled. What does it actually mean?
cards.a: Debatable — or rendered irrelevant. Context decides.
cards.n: A moot point was originally one for debate; the American sense drifted to one not worth debating.

cards.q: What should you do when a word you recognise is a false friend?
cards.a: Drop morphology entirely for that word and decide from context. The prefix is lying, so anything you build on it will be confidently wrong.
cards.n: This is why word parts eliminate rather than decide. They are reliable across a list and unreliable on any single member of it.

cards.q: Which words on the test mean two opposite things at once?
cards.a: Sanction (approve or penalize), cleave (split or cling), and moot (debatable or irrelevant). Context is the only thing that separates them.
cards.n: If one of these is a choice, look for the clue word in the sentence that fixes the direction. If there is no such clue, it is not the answer.

cards.q: Break down "amorphous".
cards.a: a- (without) + morph (shape) + -ous — Shapeless, vague.
cards.n: Used far more often of an argument or a plan than of a physical thing.

cards.q: Break down "anomalous".
cards.a: an- (not) + homal (even, regular) + -ous — Unexpected, irregular, not fitting the pattern.
cards.n: Science passages use it for the data point that does not fit, which is usually what the passage is about.
x: unexpected, irregular, not fitting the pattern

cards.q: Break down "ambiguous".
cards.a: ambi- (both) + ag (drive) + -ous — Open to more than one reading.
cards.n: Ambiguous is about the text; ambivalent is about the reader. The test contrasts them.
x: open to more than one reading

cards.q: Break down "ambivalent".
cards.a: ambi- (both) + val (worth, strength) + -ent — Pulled in two directions, holding mixed feelings.
cards.n: It is not the same as uncertain: an ambivalent person feels both things strongly.
x: pulled in two directions, holding mixed feelings

cards.q: Break down "admonition".
cards.a: ad- (to) + mon (warn) + -ition — A warning or a mild reprimand.
cards.n: Milder than a rebuke and firmer than advice — the tone matters when the question asks about attitude.
x: a warning or a mild reprimand

cards.q: Break down "assuage".
cards.a: ad- (to) + suav (sweet) — To soothe or ease.
cards.n: It takes grief, fear, hunger or doubt as its object, never a person.

cards.q: Break down "exacerbate".
cards.a: ex- (thoroughly) + acerb (bitter) + -ate — To make worse.
cards.n: The most reliable negative verb on the test. If a passage says an intervention exacerbated something, it backfired.

cards.q: Break down "detrimental".
cards.a: de- (away) + ter, tri (rub, wear) + -al — Causing damage, harmful.
cards.n: The wearing-away sense is real: detrimental effects accumulate rather than strike.

cards.q: Break down "discrepancy".
cards.a: dis- (apart) + crep (rattle) + -ancy — A mismatch between two accounts or figures.
cards.n: It names a gap, not an error. A passage can report a discrepancy without saying who is wrong.
x: a mismatch between two accounts or figures

cards.q: Break down "disparate".
cards.a: dis- (apart) + par (equal) — Fundamentally different, not comparable.
cards.n: Stronger than various or diverse: disparate things do not belong on the same scale.

cards.q: Break down "incongruous".
cards.a: in- (not) + congru (agree) + -ous — Out of place, not fitting its surroundings.
cards.n: It is about a mismatch with context, which is why it turns up in questions about tone.
x: out of place, not fitting its surroundings

cards.q: Break down "innocuous".
cards.a: in- (not) + noc (harm) + -ous — Harmless.
cards.n: Often used of something that looks dangerous and is not, so it usually answers a sentence with a contrast in it.

cards.q: Break down "insolvency".
cards.a: in- (not) + solv (loosen, pay) + -ency — Inability to pay debts.
cards.n: Solvent means able to loosen your obligations, which is why the word means both dissolving and paying.

cards.q: Break down "evacuating".
cards.a: e- (out) + vac (empty) + -ing — Emptying out.
cards.n: Science passages use it of gas or air, not only of buildings.

cards.q: Break down "elicit".
cards.a: e- (out) + licit (entice) — To draw out a response.
cards.n: Not to be confused with illicit (unlawful), which is a different word entirely.

cards.q: Break down "extricate".
cards.a: ex- (out) + tric (entanglements) + -ate — To free from a difficulty.
cards.n: The tric- is the same as in intricate: tangles. You extricate from a tangle.

cards.q: Break down "eschew".
cards.a: no useful breakdown — To deliberately avoid or abstain from.
cards.n: One of the handful of words with nothing to decode. Learn it whole and move on.
x: to deliberately avoid or abstain from

cards.q: Break down "imbue".
cards.a: in-, im- (into) + bue (soak) — To fill or saturate with a quality.
cards.n: Note the in- here means into, not not. A work imbued with grief is full of it.
x: to fill or saturate with a quality

cards.q: Break down "incipient".
cards.a: in- (into) + cip (take) + -ent — Just beginning, in its earliest stage.
cards.n: It marks something that has started but is not yet visible in full — often the thesis of a science passage.
x: just beginning, in its earliest stage

cards.q: Break down "intrinsic".
cards.a: intra- (within) — Inherent, belonging to the thing itself.
cards.n: Its opposite, extrinsic, comes from outside. Passages about motivation use the pair constantly.
x: inherent, belonging to the thing itself

cards.q: Break down "idiosyncratic".
cards.a: idio- (one's own) + syn- (together) + crat — Peculiar to one individual.
cards.n: It is neutral, not an insult: an idiosyncratic method is simply nobody else's method.

cards.q: Break down "malicious".
cards.a: mal- (bad) + -ious — Intending harm.
cards.n: Mal- makes it about intent, which is stronger than merely harmful.

cards.q: Break down "mutable".
cards.a: mut (change) + -able — Subject to change.
cards.n: Immutable is its opposite and the more common test word.

cards.q: Break down "negligible".
cards.a: neg- (not) + leg (pick, read) + -ible — Too small to be worth counting.
cards.n: Literally, not worth picking up. It is a judgement about significance, not size alone.
x: too small to be worth counting

cards.q: Break down "nominal".
cards.a: nom (name) + -al — In name only; or so small as to be trivial.
cards.n: Both senses appear. A nominal fee is tiny; a nominal leader holds the title and no power.
x: in name only; or so small as to be trivial

cards.q: Break down "obsolete".
cards.a: ob- (away) + sol (accustomed) — No longer in use.
cards.n: Obsolescent means only beginning to go out of use. The test has used the difference.

cards.q: Break down "orthodox".
cards.a: ortho- (straight, correct) + dox (opinion) — Conventional, generally accepted.
cards.n: Heterodox is its opposite. Neither one says whether the belief is true.

cards.q: Break down "paradoxical".
cards.a: para- (contrary to) + dox (opinion) + -ical — Seemingly self-contradictory.
cards.n: A paradox looks impossible and may still be true, which is what makes it worth a passage.

cards.q: Break down "perpetuating".
cards.a: per- (through) + pet (seek) + -ate — Causing something to continue.
cards.n: Almost always used of something the writer wishes would stop.

cards.q: Break down "pertinent".
cards.a: per- (thoroughly) + tin (hold) + -ent — Relevant to the matter at hand.
cards.n: It holds through to the point. Impertinent, its negative, drifted to mean rude.
x: relevant to the matter at hand

cards.q: Break down "precipitating".
cards.a: pre- (before) + cip (head) + -ate — Triggering, bringing on suddenly.
cards.n: Headlong is the image: the thing that throws events forward before anyone is ready.

cards.q: Break down "preclude".
cards.a: pre- (before) + clud (shut) — To prevent in advance, to rule out.
cards.n: Stronger than prevent: it closes the door before the attempt is made.
x: to prevent in advance, to rule out

cards.q: Break down "prescient".
cards.a: pre- (before) + sci (know) + -ent — Knowing in advance.
cards.n: Always a compliment, and usually applied in hindsight to someone who was right early.

cards.q: Break down "prevalent".
cards.a: pre- (before) + val (strength) + -ent — Widespread, common.
cards.n: It reports frequency, not approval — a prevalent belief may still be wrong.

cards.q: Break down "prolific".
cards.a: pro- (forth) + lif, fic (make) — Highly productive.
cards.n: Used of writers, artists and species. It counts output, not quality.

cards.q: Break down "rectify".
cards.a: rect (straight) + -ify — To set right, to correct.
cards.n: It implies something was crooked and has been straightened, not merely changed.

cards.q: Break down "reconcile".
cards.a: re- (again) + con- (together) + cil (call) — To make two accounts both true, or to restore agreement.
cards.n: Science passages use the first sense: reconciling two results that seem to conflict.
x: to make two accounts both true, or to restore agreement

cards.q: Break down "refute".
cards.a: re- (back) + fut (beat) — To disprove.
cards.n: To refute is to succeed. To rebut is only to answer. The test distinguishes them.

cards.q: Break down "replicate".
cards.a: re- (again) + plic (fold) + -ate — To repeat or reproduce.
cards.n: In a science passage, replication is the test of a result, not a copy of a thing.

cards.q: Break down "rescind".
cards.a: re- (back) + scind (cut) — To cancel or revoke.
cards.n: It applies to decisions, orders and laws, not to objects.

cards.q: Break down "resilient".
cards.a: re- (back) + sil (jump) + -ent — Able to recover after difficulty.
cards.n: The jumping-back image is exact: it is about return, not about strength.

cards.q: Break down "rudimentary".
cards.a: rudi (rough, raw) + -mentary — Basic, undeveloped.
cards.n: It can be neutral (an early stage) or critical (not developed enough). Tone decides.

cards.q: Break down "salient".
cards.a: sal (jump) + -ent — Standing out, most noticeable.
cards.n: The salient point is the one that leaps at you, which is why it means most important here.

cards.q: Break down "scrutinize".
cards.a: scrut (search) + -ize — To examine closely.
cards.n: From searching through rubbish for something worth keeping — the thoroughness is the point.

cards.q: Break down "substantiate".
cards.a: sub- (under) + stant (stand) + -ate — To support with evidence.
cards.n: Unsubstantiated is the commoner test word, and it is always a criticism.

cards.q: Break down "superfluous".
cards.a: super- (over) + flu (flow) + -ous — More than is needed.
cards.n: Overflowing is a fault here, not abundance — the word is a criticism.

cards.q: Break down "supplant".
cards.a: sup-, sub- (under) + plant — To replace or displace, usually by force.
cards.n: It carries the sense of taking a place that belonged to something else.
x: to replace or displace, usually by force

cards.q: Break down "supplement".
cards.a: sup-, sub- (under) + ple (fill) — To add to, to fill out.
cards.n: Compare supplant: one adds to a thing, the other removes it. One letter of difference in the middle.
x: to add to, to fill out

cards.q: Break down "tenuous".
cards.a: tenu (thin) + -ous — Weak, flimsy, barely holding.
cards.n: It describes connections, claims and grips — anything that could be stretched until it breaks.

cards.q: Break down "trivial".
cards.a: tri- (three) + via (road) — Commonplace, unimportant.
cards.n: From the three-road crossing where everyone met, so what was said there was common talk.

cards.q: Break down "ubiquitous".
cards.a: ubique (everywhere) + -ous — Found everywhere.
cards.n: It is a claim about spread, not about importance.

cards.q: Break down "undermine".
cards.a: under + mine (dig) — To weaken from beneath.
cards.n: The image is a tunnel dug under a wall. It is gradual and hidden, which is why it fits arguments.

cards.q: Break down "unprecedented".
cards.a: un- (not) + pre- (before) + ced (go) — Never having happened before.
cards.n: Three pieces, all of them common. If you can read this one, the method is working.

cards.q: Break down "viable".
cards.a: vi (life) + -able — Capable of working or surviving.
cards.n: In biology it means able to live; in an argument passage it means a plan that could actually work.

cards.q: Break down "vulnerability".
cards.a: vulner (wound) + -able + -ity — Openness to harm.
cards.n: Three pieces stacked: wound, able to be, the state of.

cards.q: What are the steps of the sixty-second method for a Words in Context question?
cards.a: One: read the sentence and decide whether the blank is positive or negative. Two: strike the choices whose prefix carries the wrong charge. Three: check what part of speech the slot needs and strike the wrong forms. Four: use the root on whatever survives and match its direction to the clue word. Five: if a survivor is a false friend, drop morphology and go to context. Six: after about thirty seconds, guess from connotation, flag it and move on.
cards.n: The order matters. Charge is the cheapest test and kills the most choices, so it goes first.
x: charge, part of speech, root, context, guess

cards.q: Because the evidence rested on a single blurry photograph, the prosecutor case was ______. Work through corroborated, tenuous, meticulous, prescient.
cards.a: The clue is negative, so corroborated (co- plus robor, strength), meticulous and prescient all go. The blank follows "was" and needs an adjective, which tenuous is. Tenu means thin: thin evidence. The answer is tenuous, in about twelve seconds.
cards.h: → eliminate, then confirm with the root
cards.n: Notice that three choices died on charge alone and the root was only needed to confirm the survivor.

cards.q: The fee is merely ______ — a few cents per transaction. Work through nominal, negligible, detrimental, punitive.
cards.a: Detrimental and punitive die immediately on charge, because "merely a few cents" is minimizing. Morphology cannot separate nominal (in name only) from negligible (too small to count) — that is a meaning call. A fee that exists but barely matters is nominal.
cards.h: → what the method kills, and where it stops
cards.n: This is the honest limit of the technique: it got you to a coin flip in five seconds, and the last step still needs vocabulary.

cards.q: Why does the method check the grammatical slot before it uses the roots?
cards.a: Because the slot is faster and more certain. A blank after "the" needs a noun, and no amount of root knowledge changes that — so the suffix test removes choices at no cost before you spend attention on meaning.
cards.n: Every step of the method is ordered by cost. Do the free eliminations first and spend your thinking on what is left.
x: it is faster and more certain

cards.q: Mark each positive or negative: benevolent, obstreperous, eulogize, disparage, munificent, malfeasance, propitious, antipathy, ameliorate, deprecate.
cards.a: Positive: benevolent, eulogize, munificent, propitious, ameliorate. Negative: obstreperous, disparage, malfeasance, antipathy, deprecate.
cards.n: You should be able to do all ten in under fifteen seconds without knowing what four of them mean. That is the whole skill.

cards.q: Give the part of speech: substantiate, substantive, substantiation. Then ambivalence and ambivalent. Then rectify and rectitude.
cards.a: Verb, adjective, noun. Then noun and adjective. Then verb and noun.
cards.n: Same root, three slots. Form, Structure and Sense questions are built out of exactly this.

cards.q: Break down: circumspect, perspicacious, intractable, magnanimous, convoluted, desultory, equivocal, obfuscate.
cards.a: Circum (around) plus spec (look) is cautious. Per (thoroughly) plus spic (see) is keenly perceptive. In (not) plus tract (pull) plus -able is stubborn. Magn (great) plus anim (soul) is generous in spirit. Con (together) plus volut (roll) is twisted and overly complex. De (away) plus sult (jump) is aimless. Equi (equal) plus voc (voice) is ambiguous or evasive. Ob (over) plus fusc (dark) is to make unclear.
cards.n: Every one of these is two pieces you already know. Nothing here needs a dictionary.

cards.q: Which mean the opposite of what they look like: invaluable, indefensible, inflammable, incontrovertible, ingenuous?
cards.a: Invaluable (extremely valuable), inflammable (burns easily) and ingenuous (naive, not "not genuine"). Indefensible and incontrovertible mean exactly what they look like.
cards.h: → the three, and why the other two are safe
cards.n: Three out of five is roughly the rate at which in- lies. It is common enough that you check the root every time.

cards.q: What is the rule for learning roots so they survive to test day?
cards.a: Never learn a root without an example word attached. About fifteen a day, each one carried by a word you can actually picture, beats a long list learned bare.
cards.n: A root with no word attached is a fact you will not retrieve under time pressure. The word is the handle.

cards.q: What do you write in your review log when you miss a vocabulary question?
cards.a: The word and its breakdown. If the word has no useful breakdown, write "memorize" beside it and move on — some words simply have to be learned whole.
cards.h: → what to record, and the exception
cards.n: The exception is not a failure of the method. It is the method telling you which words it cannot help with.

cards.q: Name some words that simply have to be memorized whole.
cards.a: Eschew, loath, regale and belie. None of them yields anything useful to a prefix or a root.
cards.n: Keeping a short list of these is worth more than trying to force a breakdown that is not there.
